headline: Parks Commission recommended the updated Vegetation Ordinance and approved $108,000 for an Ecosystem Services Analysis.
summary: The Commission reviewed and recommended approval of the updated Vegetation Ordinance, discussed off-leash dog rules without taking action, and approved Conservation Legacy Fund spending for an Ecosystem Services Analysis. Commissioners also selected committee members, re-elected leadership, and received updates on Waterfront Park events and the Comprehensive Plan.
decisions: Approved adoption of the consent agenda, including August meeting minutes and special use permits for Battery Park (Pride Parade Fest) and Calahan Park (BFC Jamboree).
Recommended approval of the Vegetation Ordinance as written and advanced it to the next body, with consideration of additional action policy.
Approved use of $108,000 in Conservation Legacy Fund money to support the Ecosystem Services Analysis.
Nominated Mamo and Davis to the Nature Based Climate Solutions Grant Review Committee, with Lantieri as alternate.
Elected Lantieri as Chair and Boehm as Vice Chair.

decision_evidence.quote: Boehm made a motion to adopt the consent agenda. Bergmann seconded. All were in favor, none opposed.

Mobley made a motion to approve the vegetation ordinance as written and advance it to the next body and recommends considering additional action policy. Mamo seconded. All were in favor, none opposed.
Boehm made a motion to approve the use of Conservation Legacy Fund funds to support the Ecosystem Services Analysis. Bergmann seconded. All were in favor, none opposed.
Boehm made a motion to nominate Mamo and Davis with Lantieri as an alternate, Mobley seconded. All were in favor, none opposed.
Bergmann made a motion to nominate Lantieri as Chair and Boehm as Vice Chair, Mamo seconded. All were in favor, none opposed.

plain_text:
Parks Commission Meeting 
September 8th, 2026 at 5:30pm 
645 Pine St., Front Conference Room & Zoom 
Staff in Attendance: Lewis, Sauve, Cahill, Gustin, Doyle & O’Daniel 
Commissioners in Attendance: Lantieri, Boehm, Mobley, Davis, Bergmann & Mamo 
Lantieri opened the meeting at 5:35pm by welcoming everyone.  
1. Agenda 
1.1 Motion to amend/adopt agenda 
Mobley made a motion to adopt the agenda. Boehm seconded. All were in favor, none 
opposed.  
 
2. Consent Agenda 
2.1 August Meeting Minutes 
2.2 Battery Park Special Use Permit Request (Pride Parade Fest) 
2.3 Calahan Park Special Use Permit Request (BFC Jamboree) 
Boehm made a motion to adopt the consent agenda. Bergmann seconded. All were in 
favor, none opposed.  
 
3. Public Forum – Time Certain, 6pm 
3.1 Verbal Comments 
Public forum was opened at 6:17pm. 
KJ Doyle, BPRW’s Event Manager, was present to give an update about the Waterfront 
Park event season. She began by reviewing the successful season so far, noting that all 
events that were ticketed saw higher ticket sales this year than the last few years. She 
shared that the return of the Higher Ground concert series was fantastic. Doyle then 
touched on the final 3 upcoming events at Waterfront Park – Grace Potter’s Grand Point 
North event, which has had strong ticket sales so far, followed by a Flynn event and then 
a new event called Mojo Burlington. She continued that this is a grassroots concert and 
festival production company focused on local music, artists and businesses and they 
have been working diligently with BPRW to make this event happen here in Burlington. 
She shared that she is excited to bring another large scale event to Waterfront Park 
because those increase the Department’s ability to support smaller events across the 
City. Doyle also noted that fundraising walk/run events are about to kick off for the 
season.  
Lantieri offered volunteer support if needed at any point. 
Doyle responded that these events are all set but that she would be in touch about her 
Halloween event soon! 
With no one else present, public forum was closed at 6:21pm. 
4. Deliberative Agenda 
4.1 Vegetation Ordinance Overview and Approvals
Gustin began by sharing his screen and giving a brief overview. He shared that they were 
there to get the Commission’s recommendation for approval of this ordinance. He 
shared that they have incorporated as many of the comments received so far as best 
they were able to and if approved tonight they will proceed to the Conservation Board 
next week and are aiming to bring it to City Council at the end of the month, with 
anticipation that it will be referred to their ordinance committee in October.  
Cahill noted that an exciting addition to the process will be a public meeting on the 21st 
where community members will be invited to come and learn about the ordinance and 
the amendments that are being made. He shared his excitement to utilize this as an 
educational opportunity as well as some tree giveaways. Cahill shared that he feels this 
ordinance is going to strengthen a lot of Burlington’s unique characters in terms of the 
rare natural community types that exist across the landscape in the urban forest and the 
shade trees that line the streets and that it feels like a celebration as well as having 
some measures in place to protect those.  
Gustin shared that the current ordinance is missing a lot, and the goal of the update is to 
establish and maintain diversity in age and species in trees that make up Burlington’s 
Urban Forest, as well as broaden diversity in native species of vegetation in the open 
spaces. He continued that this applies City-wide, including public property as well as 
institutional and private properties. He shared that the existing ordinance was adopted 
in 1962 and most recently amended in 1995 and had some basic standards around 
burning and removing trees on public property, but not much else. Gustin continued by 
listing the changes that have happened between now and 1995, including the Open 
Space Protection Plan adopted in 2000, the creation of the Conservation Legacy Fund a 
few years after that, a Climate Action Plan that was adopted in 2010, the reality of 
climate change being real and not being able to meet emission targets globally so 
shifting to focus on resiliency and adaptation instead, and the brand new Open Space 
Plan that was adopted earlier this year, which specifically called out updating the 
Vegetation Ordinance as an action item. Gustin continued that Burlington’s green 
spaces have contributed to climate resiliency, biodiversity, water quality and overall 
quality of life for the community. He then shared some facts and figures that came in 
large part from the spatial analysis lab work that was done as a part of the Open Space 
Plan recently, noting that there is currently 40% tree canopy cover which is a slight 
decrease of about 1.5% from 2014, which includes about 228 acres of gain but 337 acres 
of loss in that time frame, hence the slight net decrease. He continued by sharing that 
the canopy is unevenly distributed throughout the City, as is the tree loss and gains.  
Cahill chimed in that at one point in time there was a goal connected to the City’s 
Climate Action Plan from 2008 and the only nature-based aspect of that plan was tree 
planting until 50% tree canopy was achieved, which would be roughly the equivalent of 
trying to return all of the farmland at the Intervale to canopy. He continued that while it 
isn’t a good sign that Burlington is losing canopy, the heart of this update is keeping the 
canopy that exists and helping it grow stronger.  
Richards noted that cities in general struggle to maintain tree canopy because it tends 
to get lost in places where they don’t have control, which is important to keep in mind 
here in Burlington. She continued that the updated ordinance tries to help with this.
Cahill continued that the ordinance alone is not going to get Burlington to where it 
needs to go but the educational and active stewardship aspects of the Open Space Plan 
is a good vehicle to help with that, so they are two pieces that work well together. He 
continued that the idea of encouraging active, daily stewardship is what will support 
these efforts. He used the example of stewardship zones that protect and buffer natural 
areas, which can be used as a tool for encouraging that type of regular community 
stewardship, so the timing of updating key things like the vegetation ordinance while 
rolling out opportunities for the community to engage is vital.    
Gustin then shared a slide about the number of trees planted and removed from green 
belts and parks over the past 15 years or so – 3,104 trees planted, 2,684 trees removed 
and 1,933 trees planted from the Branch Out Burlington nursery. He then asked Cahill 
how many trees the Conservation Team has planted.  
Cahill shared that for the same number of years, it was probably closer to 10-15,000, 
but they primarily plan restoration trees which have a 40-70% survivability rate 
compared to heftier bare root trees, so a different methodology.  
Mobley asked if the trees planted from the Branch Out Burlington nursery were a subset 
of the total trees planted.  
Cahill and Gustin answered subset.  
Gustin continued by sharing a map of the existing tree canopy percentages throughout 
Burlington, noting that there are less trees downtown compared to natural areas. He 
continued that the urban forest helps to strengthen and retain the green fabric of the 
community while also accommodating housing growth, which is going to be a key factor 
moving forward. He then shared a map of the amount of loss and gain of tree canopy, 
noting some specific locations with projects that account for the higher percentages of 
loss. Gustin continued by sharing the high level objectives of the amended vegetation 
ordinance including housekeeping items, introducing definitions, jurisdiction and 
authority, referencing the State statute where applicable including designating a Tree 
Warden and Deputy Tree Warden, flushing out in greater detail private owner 
responsibilities along public streets and sidewalks and follow-up when that is needed 
and the Conservation Board’s role in that. He continued that the introduction of 
mitigation measures when trees are removed on private property has also been added 
and consists of 3 pieces – the caliper for caliper replacement either on-site or off-site, 
payment or on-site green infrastructure to handle the ten year storm standard. 
Mamo asked what portion of the 40% of tree canopy is public vs. private property.  
Richards, Gustin and Cahill all noted those specifics are outlined in the Open Space Plan.  
Mamo asked if the ordinance could be an opportunity to improve the decision-making 
process around how public trees are managed. He noted that the way it is written right 
now gives complete control to the City Arborist in terms of management plans and 
removal decisions and he was curious if this could be a good way to have a more robust 
decision-making process around the removal process.  
Gustin responded that the City Arborist does not actually have complete control over it. 
He continued that public trees are in two boxes – shade trees, which are all street trees 
and intentionally planted trees in parks, and the State statute outlines the process that 
the City needs to follow for those, including public events. He shared that there are
some exceptions to this, including a tree that is infested or a tree that is a public hazard 
or a removal necessary to complete a City project. Gustin continued that the other box 
are trees in open spaces, which would likely be part of an annual work plan for City staff, 
which would go through the Conservation Board. 
Cahill noted that he felt it would be useful to follow this new ordinance especially when 
it comes to this piece and to have the Conservation Board create a space to discuss 
what is in the work plans, encouraging participation as a check and balance and also as 
an opportunity to support where the limitations are by thinking outside of the box. He 
continued that he believes once the Tree Board is established and functioning, that it 
could be a great space for that.  
Gustin shared that in order to get this up and running, there needs to be more general 
standards versus more specific because the tighter the box you’re in the less 
maneuverability you have, so if you start with a bigger box you have the flexibility to 
move, adjust and adapt in the coming years to see how it is working and what might 
need to be adjusted and fine-tuned. He continued that he believes what Mamo is 
getting at can be enabled through this but isn’t specifically called out and he feels that it 
doesn’t need to be. 
Mamo responded that from a governance perspective to have the jurisdiction language 
in the ordinance give the City Arborist complete control and authority is a lot to be 
granted to one individual. He continued that from a property value perspective, an 
environmental perspective, a neighborhood perspective, to have even the most 
qualified individual be able to have the final say seems like there is room for 
improvement in that structure by including somebody like the Conservation Board to 
review those plans. He acknowledged that there had been a section added in regards to 
this, but it doesn’t have any parameters or say that it will include plans to remove trees 
or plans to change management strategies.  
Gustin responded that this is the ordinance built off of the Open Space Plan which now 
includes the Urban Forest Plan that used to be separate. He continued that it’s actually 
City Council who has the ultimate call in regards to shade trees and everything that is 
not a shade tree depends and if it is a public tree, it is probably Comai or Cahill, but if it’s 
trees on private property it would go through a zoning process.    
Lantieri chimed in that he feels the heart of this conversation is coming from hearing 
from community members about tree removals and asking what options they have. He 
acknowledge that creating this process gets more towards creating space for that but it 
doesn’t call that out specifically. Lantieri continued that he hears it both ways – that 
there is value in keeping it open so that it can mold into the right thing and that this is 
something that consistently comes up with community members after the removal has 
happened. He feels there is something to the idea of notifications and the ability to have 
space for people to hear what is happening ahead of time, and whether that is defined 
in the way that the Conservation Board is empowered as the Tree Committee is the 
question. 
Gustin then shared the current State statute, noting that this is the current law whether 
this ordinance ends up being adopted or not and it includes the exceptions for shade 
tree removals that have been discussed.
Cahill shared that he could not recall a time that a tree was removed when it wasn’t for 
one of the two exceptions, infestation and/or a hazard.  
Lantieri agreed that this is tricky because things like the ash removal are because of an 
infestation issue.  
Davis asked how a resident on a street is made aware that a tree is going to be 
removed. 
Cahill responded that tree work is noticed on-site with signage. 
Lewis noted that if it is a street tree, they notice in the days leading up to the work for 
no-parking in the area and the purpose is noted on the signage for that.  
Cahill anecdotally shared that he was not aware any removals that have happened that 
were not related to an infrastructure project or an infestation or a hazard, which under 
law do not require notice. He continued that regardless, what he noted earlier about 
educational every day stewardship and where Burlington moves forward as a 
community with climate resiliency and nature connection, awareness is vital.  
Mobley chimed in to clarify that trees are removed for 2 primary reasons – 
infestation/hazard and infrastructure. She shared that while she is fully behind the 
educational and awareness pieces that are being discussed, she wants to keep the 
realities of City resources in mind when talking about adding in processes. She then 
asked if a tree is infested, is the only option to remove it. 
Cahill answered that there is potentially an inoculation route.  
Mobley responded that while that may work, it becomes an equity question when some 
neighborhoods have the people and time to focus on that while others do not. She 
continued that there is a real opportunity for more communication and education but 
she doesn’t feel that the ordinance needs to be changed to achieve that.  
Lewis responded that there is an opportunity to evaluate and adjust the standard 
operating procedures and process for staff through an updated Department policy, 
while being cognizant of staff work plans and administrative time.  
Cahill noted that this is where the Tree Board has the opportunity to be present with all 
of those processes and have an active participation and partnership in it. 
After a brief pause for Public Forum, Mamo reflected that if most of the removals occur 
because of infestation or hazards then having a more robust oversight process wouldn’t 
really impact the day to day operations but instead the more rare instances that don’t 
fall into those categories.  
Gustin shared that they can’t make the Conservation Board an appeal board but under 
the State statute, appeals would go to City Council where the public can weigh in. He 
continued that there is also an appeal process to the Superior Court environmental 
division of the Vermont Supreme Court, so the hierarchy has been figured out for all 
scenarios. Gustin reiterated that he feels having a bigger box as opposed to a smaller 
box right now will be helpful.  
Lantieri suggested that this body could potentially work with the Conservation Board on 
the policy level stuff. He continued that being proactive in these kinds of situations, 
even if it is short notice for something like an infestation, could be helpful across the 
board. He shared that finding a middle ground in the policy that is cognizant of the
reality of staff time and provide people the opportunity to be brought into the 
conversation.  
Mamo thanked everyone for tailoring his questions and noted that the only comments 
he has received from community members since becoming a Commissioner have been 
related to tree removals. He continued that his Ward was significantly impacted by the 
ash tree removals and a lot of folks have been asking why they weren’t able to give their 
input and asking if there were options other than removing them.  
Richards chimed in that hopefully moving forward there will be a more diversified tree 
canopy to avoid major and concentrated removals due to infestations in the future. She 
then noted that people feel a lot of grief when trees are removed.  
Cahill agreed and shared his sentiments that it is important to provide a space for the 
community to feel and work through that grief.  
Mobley highlighted the theme that she heard throughout the conversation, which 
included more proactive communication ahead of time. 
Richards noted that there has been a lot of complexity in these moments because while 
there has been a lot of communication about the ash trees, a disconnect she has 
experienced is that some people don’t know what an ash tree looks like. 
Cahill noted that when there is loss, there is emotion and Burlington is a community 
that gets hyped, which can lead to debates that take time and energy from all sides. He 
continued by sharing that he feels there should be spaces created where people can 
process these feelings and build community around thinking of generative solutions 
about how they want to support their neighborhoods and the City overall. He then 
shared that this is an exciting opportunity to trial some different approaches.   
Mobley made a motion to approve the vegetation ordinance as written and advance it 
to the next body and recommends considering additional action policy. Mamo 
seconded. 
All were in favor, none opposed.  
4.2 Legacy Fund Funding Approval – Ecosystem Services Analysis 
Gustin opened that this is for an Ecosystem Services Analysis by Trust for Public Land. He 
gave a brief background noting that the 2022 nature-based climate solution and 2026 
Open Space Plan both talked a lot about resiliency and ecosystem services and with the 
City currently updating its Comprehensive Plan, the analysis that is proposed here could 
help inform decision making as well as anticipated redesign standards that will be 
worked on after the comp plan is adopted. He continued that there are 2 basic pieces of 
the study – quantifying the economic benefits of ecosystem services with 3 focal areas: 
storm water management, air pollution removal and nature-based climate solutions and 
the other major aspect will be the climate cooling effect for open spaces, primarily the 
urban forest. Gustin shared that the project is expected to take about 9 months and the 
funding ask from the Legacy Fund is $108,000. He continued that if approved, it will go 
to the Conservation Board next week and then Board of Finance. He then shared the 
hope that this would help inform the Comprehensive Plan.  
Mobley shared that she thinks this is really exciting and to have this information for the 
Comprehensive Plan is critical during this decision making time.
Richards noted that there are so many ways to build infrastructure and to have some 
valuing of the importance of green infrastructure is truly valuable.  
Boehm made a motion to approve the use of Conservation Legacy Fund funds to 
support the Ecosystem Services Analysis. Bergmann seconded.  
All were in favor, none opposed.  
4.3 Nature Based Climate Solutions Grant Review Committee 
Cahill opened by sharing that this will be the 4th round of the grants and noted that this 
is an exciting opportunity for the Conservation Board and Parks Commission to work 
together in a subcommittee to review and award them. He continued by sharing that 
this has been and will continue to be a meaningful and well organized process.  
Mobley shared that is was a great opportunity and a fun way to learn.  
Davis shared that she would be happy to do it again because she thought it was a great 
process and enjoyed evaluating everything with the metrics that were provided.  
Lantieri opened the floor for interested Commissioners to self-nominate.  
Cahill noted that the commitment involves 2 meetings and some individual time needed 
to read and score the applications leading up to those.  
Lantieri shared that he was interested, but only if others were not. 
Mamo noted that he was interested. 
Davis noted that she was interested.  
Boehm made a motion to nominate Mamo and Davis with Lantieri as an alternate, 
Mobley seconded. All were in favor, none opposed.  
4.4 Appendix D, Section 7 
Lantieri opened this item by explaining that Appendix D is the main place in the 
ordinance that governs park rules and section 7 is in relation to off-leash dogs. He 
continued that there was a pilot that expired and the Commission has done some work 
to update it but it hasn’t been finalized. He noted that they would not be taking any 
action on it at this meeting. 
Lewis began by sharing that they would be looking at multiple ordinance updates over 
time but noted that vehicles in parks has been tabled for now as broader conversations 
about what that could look like and how the ordinance should be updated to reflect that 
are happening. He continued that today would entail a broad overview of off-leash dogs 
with action at a future meeting. He began by sharing that after the last discussion on 
this topic, the clean version was forwarded to the City Attorney’s office for review, who 
had feedback. One of the major pieces was removing the policy so that it is separate 
from the ordinance, and can just be approved by this body in the future instead of being 
codified in the ordinance. Lewis was open to feedback however the group wanted to 
proceed but specifically noted that the lawyers had a few recommendations regarding 
referring to the Director as the chief general authority for closing parks and identifying 
specific use of funds taken in for commercial use of the dog parks to be used for 
improvements to the dog parks.  
Lantieri felt that they could get a cleaned up version of this done offline by the next 
meeting.  
Lewis shared that an off-leash pilot project has been happening in a specific section at 
Leddy Beach and some questions and concerns came up when the signage was recently
revamped. He shared that he spent some time there and only saw 1 older dog there 
using the space respectfully and when he asked the owner about any issues they said 
that they are there regularly and had never experienced any conflicts.  
Boehm noted a line about no off-leash areas designated in unfenced areas, would that 
make it so that the pilot actually isn’t allowed? 
Lewis answered that that would be a good question for the attorney. 
Boehm continued that below that there was a line about other areas may be designated 
as off-leash areas as per the policy, but she assumed that meant fenced.  
Lantieri chimed in that this is essentially where things had been left off last time and the 
reality is that if they don’t approve any off-leash areas people will still bring their dogs 
into the lake without leashes.  
Lewis noted that it is typically better when there are alternative locations for this kind of 
thing, so identifying an area where it can happen would probably be best. 
Mamo asked about Texaco Beach and Starr Farm Beach. 
Lantieri answered that technically those would be excluded. He continued that the main 
issue right now is that the ordinance is expired, so there are essentially no rules 
regarding off-leash dogs right now, just this shell of defunct language. He reminded 
everyone that during the last discussion, the direction the group had been leaning was 
to not have any unfenced, off-leash areas, so this would be a change of intent that is 
worth considering. He noted that this is the only substantive decision that they would 
need to come to as a body and then ultimately when it gets passed on to other bodies, 
there could be changes made.  
Boehm liked the idea of having off-leash areas in the policy so that there would be 
flexibility with changes as needed, so keeping the ordinance vague as fenced and 
unfenced areas and that they are outlined in the policy.  
There was general agreement from the group. 
Lantieri was in agreement but shared his concerns about where these policies live and 
how they can be accessed by the public.  
Lewis said he has identified that on the general BPRW work plan to address.  
Lantieri summarized the action items, noting that the ordinance needs to be cleaned up, 
some of the specifics need to be moved into the policy and getting the policy into a 
place that they all want it to be.  
Lewis asked the group to do some thinking on the water access piece specifically.  
4.5 Commission Member Chair, Foundation Seat Selection 
Lantieri opened this item by letting Commissioners know anyone can self-nominate or 
nominate others for the Chair, Vice Chair and Parks Foundation seat.  
Mobley nominated Lantieri to continue in the role of Chair. 
No one else showed interest in the position. 
Boehm, the current Vice Chair, encouraged others to consider the role because while 
she was happy to continue in it, she wanted someone who was maybe interested in the 
Chair role eventually to have the opportunity to engage with this position first.  
Mobley nominated Boehm to be the Vice Chair. 
Lantieri asked if anyone was interested in serving in the Parks Foundation seat, which he 
shared entails a meeting every other month and reporting back to this group.
Mobley asked if the role involved fundraising. 
Lantieri answered that there is no requirement to. 
Mobley said she would like to attend the next meeting and would make a decision after.  
Bergmann made a motion to nominate Lantieri as Chair and Boehm as Vice Chair, Mamo 
seconded.  
All were in favor, none opposed.  
4.6 Comprehensive Plan Update 
Sauve wanted to provide everyone with updates and some background in terms of 
leadership, engagement and data to inform some of the decisions and conversations at 
a meeting being held the next day. She began by sharing the draft slides for BPRW’s 
overall data, which notes parks, facilities etc., and she feels is especially interesting 
when compared to the national standards, of which BPRW is larger than most cities of a 
similar size. She reminded everyone that when Plan BTV 2050 is being discussed that 
adding 7,000 new housing units to the City is a piece of that, so there is a question 
about how that will impact things. She continued by sharing the public engagement 
summary, referencing the work the interns who presented last month did as well as the 
open house in April, other engagement events, various surveys and staff engagement 
with the process. All of these opportunities have given residents the chance to share 
what is special about BPRW, concerns/feedback and ideas. She called out that the 
quality of and access to parks, nature and the lake has been resoundingly positive and 
important to people who live here. She continued that overall residents are very 
satisfied with the BPRW system, but there are some gaps, like indoor recreation 
locations and outdoor swimming areas. It was found that New American residents are 
more likely to express dissatisfaction with a lot of the components, but the majority are 
satisfied with some of the elements. Sauve continued that while residents are generally 
satisfied with sports fields, courts and playgrounds, outdoor restrooms are at the 
bottom in terms of if needs are met. She then shared a slide about combining “need” 
and “importance”, which indicated a priority for restrooms, swimming areas, trails, 
indoor recreation and art. She continued by sharing that special events and recreational 
programs were at the top of the list for “need” and “importance”. She continued by 
noting that in terms of barriers, most residents said that they do not know what is 
offered which the 2015 plan also indicated, which is where the marketing position and 
the new logo came from, so the Department needs to dig into why this still seems to be 
the case, as well as other contributing factors that have been indicated. Sauve 
continued that some topics that came up throughout all of these engagements and that 
have been discussed here are safety and unhoused residents and the competing needs 
are obvious. She shared that staff also have concerns about this and they are wondering 
what residents would like the City to do. Sauve noted that while there were not any 
questions about housing developments in parks, there was feedback against that that 
came through both the surveys and direct interactions with the public. She also shared 
that they have been receiving negative feedback about fast and dangerous e-motos on 
the greenway. Sauve then shared that the values that came out of feedback from staff 
was that staff are passionate about the work they are doing and that shows in the work 
that is being done even though budgets have been cut over the years. That meeting also
showed that staff want to continue to be leaders in climate adaptation, and she pointed 
to the Vegetation Ordinance as an example of that. She continued that an underlying 
theme with staff is being stretched too thin. Next, Sauve went over the draft vision 
statement, which she noted was quite long, but asked for feedback. 
Mamo said he was looking for something in there about “preservation of existing”. 
Lantieri agreed. 
The group then briefly discussed the housing targets, which were clarified as goals not 
mandates, and what the proposals for how to that are.  
Sauve shared her assumption that the final vision statement will be shorter and 
simplified.  
Mobley feels like this version is the vision with implicit values woven in, which she feels 
need to be called out because in these conversations about the overall Plan BTV 2050 
there are going to be trade-offs, so knowing what the City’s values are in relationship to 
the vision is going to prioritize the hard choices that need to be made.  
Lantieri asked what next steps are. 
Sauve shared that it will be going to PACC for review this week, which at that point and 
after this meeting, it will be public. Then it will be shared at the next open house.  
 
5. Standing Items 
5.1 Parks Foundation Update 
Lantieri shared that there was a meeting in August and the next one is in October.  
Sauve noted that they will be doing engagement in Baird, Ethan Allen and Smalley parks 
about the playground replacements.  
5.2 Director’s Report 
Lewis pointed folks to the monthly report and currently the Department is focused on 
shifting into fall with less seasonal support.  
5.3 Commissioner’s Items & Volunteer Hours 
Mobley shared that the end of Pine St. near Baird Park is experiencing an uptick of drug 
dealing and car accidents since it has become a dead end. She noted that the hedge 
along the edge of the park is currently a hot topic. She had 2 hours to report. 
Mamo had a lot of conversations about the vegetation ordinance. He had 4 hours to 
report. 
Lantieri shared that he is continuing to work with volunteers in the Urban Reserve. He 
had 10 hours to report. 
Boehm had 1 hour to report. 
Bergmann had 1.5 hours to report. And shared the same sentiment as Mobley about the 
now dead end Pine St. 
Davis shared that she has been visiting Battery and City Hall Parks. She had 2 hours to 
report.  
 
6. Adjournment 
6.1 Motion to Adjourn 
Davis made a motion to adjourn, Mobley seconded. All were in favor, none opposed.
